card.thesis: College tuition credits use fixed income cutoffs, so a family that once qualified in full, with pay that merely kept pace with prices, now gets nothing.
card.overturns: "If our income only keeps pace with inflation, we keep qualifying for college tax credits."

claim: The American Opportunity credit (up to $2,500 per student) starts phasing out at modified AGI of $160,000 for joint filers ($80,000 single) and is gone at $180,000 ($90,000) - the same dollar amounts it had when it was created for tax year 2009, and the Lifetime Learning credit now uses the same fixed range (not adjusted since 2020). Consumer prices rose by a factor of about 1.534 from 2009 (annual average) to the 12 months ending August 2026, so the 2009 cutoff of $160,000 is about $245,388 in current prices and the 2009 end of the range, $180,000, is about $276,061. A married couple at exactly $160,000 in 2009 (full credit) whose income merely kept pace with prices now has about $245,388 and receives $0; if their income grew like U.S. median household income (from $49,780 in 2009 to $87,460 in 2025) they would have about $281,109, also $0. The start of the phase-out was 3.21 times median household income in 2009 and is 1.83 times in 2025. The $2,500 maximum would be about $3,834 if it had kept pace with prices. Tax year 2026 rules. Sources: 26 U.S.C. 25A(b), 25A(d); IRS IR-2025-103; IRS American opportunity tax credit Q&A (historical, 2009).

assumptions: Tax year 2026 rules (U.S. Code as in force 2026-09-29): phase-out $160,000-$180,000 joint, $80,000-$90,000 other filers; maximum $2,500 per student with at least $4,000 of qualifying expenses.
Price comparison uses CPI-U (seasonally adjusted, all items): 2009 calendar-year average vs the latest 12 months (Sep 2025-Aug 2026).
Median household income is the Census current-dollar median (annual); the couple example is a stylized household whose income grows exactly with prices or with the median.
MAGI is treated as equal to the couple's income.
limits: History, not a forecast. Uses a price index and a median; individual income paths differ. Tuition itself rose differently from the all-items index. No personal advice.
